# Advisory rules

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-rules-doc.ts from packages/rules. Do not edit by hand: run `npm run rules:docs`. -->

Deterministic, versioned rules turn the observations of a successful scan job into findings
(design §8). Severity and confidence come only from rule code — never from an LLM. An observation
is not a vulnerability: rule text states what was observed and why it matters, and never claims
compromise. A rule runs only when the job profile includes one of its checks and the job produced
successful observations of every kind it requires; failed, timed-out, partial or missing evidence
neither raises nor resolves a finding. A finding resolves only when its rule evaluated the same
component with successful evidence and the condition was absent.

## Risk model v1

`risk_score = clamp(round(severity_weight × exposure_factor × criticality_factor), 0, 100)`.
Severity stays separate from the risk score; the inputs are stored with every finding.

| Severity      | Weight |
| ------------- | ------ |
| informational | 5      |
| low           | 25     |
| medium        | 50     |
| high          | 75     |
| critical      | 95     |

| Exposure          | Factor |
| ----------------- | ------ |
| `public_record`   | 0.8    |
| `web`             | 1      |
| `network_service` | 1.1    |

| Domain criticality | Factor |
| ------------------ | ------ |
| low                | 0.7    |
| medium             | 0.85   |
| high               | 1      |
| critical           | 1.15   |

### ASSET-001 — Newly discovered unapproved candidate asset

| Field                      | Value         |
| -------------------------- | ------------- |
| Version                    | 1             |
| Category                   | `asset`       |
| Default severity           | informational |
| Default confidence         | medium        |
| Observation kinds required | `discovery`   |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `discovery`   |

**Evidence required.** Successful discovery observations (hostnames beneath the domain, exact label boundary) and the domain's asset list.

**Detection.** A discovered hostname is not a known asset, or is a pending candidate that nobody has approved or rejected yet. One finding per hostname (component = the hostname).

**Resolution.** The hostname has been approved, rejected or suspended in the asset inventory (evaluated on any successful discovery run).

**Sample advisory** (for `dev.example.com`): _Review the candidate asset dev.example.com_

A hostname under the domain appeared in a passive source (for example a Certificate Transparency log) and is not in the approved inventory. Unknown hosts are not monitored: forgotten services, shadow IT or third-party sites using the domain can go unpatched or be misconfigured without anyone noticing.

Recommended actions:

- Identify the owner of the hostname (DNS records, certificate details, team inventories).
- If it belongs to your organisation and you are authorised to scan it, approve it so it is monitored.
- If it is not yours or no longer used, reject it and remove stale DNS records and certificates.
- Never approve third-party hosting/CDN addresses for active scanning without the provider's permission.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6962>
- <https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/bod-23-01-improving-asset-visibility-and-vulnerability-detection-federal-networks>

### ASSET-002 — Previously monitored asset missing from a successful discovery run

| Field                      | Value       |
| -------------------------- | ----------- |
| Version                    | 1           |
| Category                   | `asset`     |
| Default severity           | medium      |
| Default confidence         | low         |
| Observation kinds required | `discovery` |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `discovery` |

**Evidence required.** A complete discovery run in the current job (every discovery observation successful) and the hostnames from the previous successful discovery run.

**Detection.** An approved, monitored asset was in the previous discovery run but not in the current one. Confidence is low: passive sources age out and vary, so absence is a prompt to check, not proof.

**Resolution.** The asset appears again in a complete discovery run, or it is no longer approved and monitored.

**Sample advisory** (for `legacy.example.com`): _Confirm the status of legacy.example.com_

A monitored asset is no longer reported by passive discovery. The asset inventory may be out of date. Decommissioned hosts left in the inventory waste monitoring effort, while DNS records left behind for removed services can become dangling and be claimed by others.

Recommended actions:

- Check whether the host still exists and still resolves (see the DNS observations of the latest scan).
- If it was decommissioned: remove its DNS records, revoke its certificates and suspend the asset.
- If it is still in service: keep monitoring; no change is required.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6962>
- <https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/bod-23-01-improving-asset-visibility-and-vulnerability-detection-federal-networks>

### DNS-001 — Unexpected authoritative DNS change

| Field                      | Value  |
| -------------------------- | ------ |
| Version                    | 1      |
| Category                   | `dns`  |
| Default severity           | medium |
| Default confidence         | high   |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`  |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`  |

**Evidence required.** Successful apex NS lookups in the current job and in the previous successful job (both non-empty); apex SOA lookups in both jobs are compared when available.

**Detection.** The apex NS set, or the SOA primary name server (MNAME), differs from the previous successful observation. There is no change-approval workflow yet, so every change is treated as unexpected until reviewed.

**Resolution.** Not auto-resolved: a change is an event that needs review, so the finding stays open until an analyst resolves or accepts it (a repeated identical observation does not undo the change). A user with `findings:triage` can also resolve it manually after review.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Review the authoritative DNS change for example.com_

The name servers (or SOA primary) answering for this domain changed since the previous successful scan. Planned DNS provider migrations look exactly like this; unplanned changes can indicate an unauthorised registrar or DNS-provider account change. Whoever controls the authoritative name servers controls web, e-mail and certificate validation for the domain. An unplanned change could redirect traffic or allow certificates to be issued to a third party.

Recommended actions:

- Confirm with the domain owner that the change was planned (change ticket, provider migration).
- If unplanned: verify the delegation at the registrar, rotate registrar and DNS-provider credentials, enable MFA, and review account audit logs.
- Enable registrar lock / registry lock where available to prevent unauthorised delegation changes.
- Compare the zone content served by the new name servers with the expected records.
- Once reviewed, resolve the finding (or accept it) in ExDomainVault.

References:

- <https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-19-01-mitigate-dns-infrastructure-tampering>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1034>
- <https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/epp-status-codes-2014-06-16-en>

### DNS-002 — Potential dangling CNAME requiring validation

| Field                      | Value  |
| -------------------------- | ------ |
| Version                    | 1      |
| Category                   | `dns`  |
| Default severity           | medium |
| Default confidence         | medium |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`  |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`  |

**Evidence required.** Successful CNAME lookup for the hostname and successful A and AAAA lookups for the same hostname (the resolver follows the CNAME chain, so they describe the final target). CNAME lookups of in-domain chain members are followed when present in the same job.

**Detection.** The hostname is a CNAME whose chain leaves the monitored domain and neither A nor AAAA returns an address (NXDOMAIN or NODATA). Confidence is medium when the target is a known takeover-prone service or the answer was NXDOMAIN, low otherwise. Nothing is probed: this needs manual validation.

**Resolution.** The CNAME lookup succeeds with no CNAME, the chain stays inside the domain, or A/AAAA now return an address.

**Sample advisory** (for `shop.example.com`): _Validate the CNAME on shop.example.com_

The hostname points at an external name that currently has no address. This is a common sign of a deprovisioned cloud or SaaS resource whose DNS alias was left behind. If another party can claim the referenced resource, they could serve content, collect cookies scoped to the parent domain, or obtain certificates for this hostname.

Recommended actions:

- Confirm whether the referenced resource still exists and is owned by your organisation.
- If it is no longer used, delete the CNAME record (and any related records) now.
- If it is still needed, re-claim the resource on azurewebsites.net under your account before re-enabling traffic.
- Make DNS cleanup part of the decommissioning checklist for cloud resources.

References:

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/subdomain-takeover>
- <https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/02-Configuration_and_Deployment_Management_Testing/10-Test_for_Subdomain_Takeover>
- <https://github.com/EdOverflow/can-i-take-over-xyz>

### DNS-003 — Missing DMARC policy

| Field                      | Value   |
| -------------------------- | ------- |
| Version                    | 1       |
| Category                   | `email` |
| Default severity           | medium  |
| Default confidence         | high    |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`   |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`   |

**Evidence required.** Successful TXT lookup at _dmarc.<apex> (NXDOMAIN/NODATA count as "no record"). The apex MX lookup, when successful, tailors the advice for domains that do not send or receive mail.

**Detection.** No TXT record at _dmarc.<apex> starts with v=DMARC1, more than one does (receivers then ignore DMARC, RFC 7489 §6.6.3), or the single record has no valid p= policy. A monitoring-only policy (p=none) is reported separately by DNS-007.

**Resolution.** Exactly one DMARC record with a valid p= policy is published at _dmarc.<apex>.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Publish a DMARC policy for example.com_

DMARC lets the domain owner tell receivers what to do with mail that fails SPF/DKIM alignment and where to send reports. Without an effective DMARC policy, phishing that impersonates the domain is more likely to reach recipients, and the owner gets no visibility into who sends mail using the domain.

Recommended actions:

- Publish one TXT record at _dmarc.example.com, starting with "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:<reporting address>" to collect reports.
- Inventory legitimate senders from the aggregate reports and align them with SPF and DKIM.
- Move to p=quarantine and then p=reject (BOD 18-01 requires p=reject for US federal domains).
- Make sure only one DMARC record exists at that name.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489>
- <https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/bod-18-01-enhance-email-and-web-security>
- <https://www.m3aawg.org/sites/default/files/m3aawg_parked_domains_bp-2015-12.pdf>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7505>

### DNS-004 — Significant SPF configuration issue

| Field                      | Value   |
| -------------------------- | ------- |
| Version                    | 1       |
| Category                   | `email` |
| Default severity           | medium  |
| Default confidence         | high    |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`   |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`   |

**Evidence required.** Successful apex TXT lookup. A missing SPF record is only reported when the apex MX lookup also succeeded and lists a mail exchanger.

**Detection.** Apex SPF (v=spf1) has: more than one record (medium, permerror); "+all" (high); malformed or unknown terms (medium); more than 10 DNS-querying terms counted at the top level only — include, a, mx, ptr, exists, redirect (medium); "?all" or no all/redirect (low); ptr (low). A domain with MX but no SPF is low. Severity is the highest of the issues found.

**Resolution.** A single, well-formed SPF record with a restrictive all (or redirect=) and at most 10 top-level lookups — or no SPF where the domain has no MX.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Fix the SPF record for example.com_

SPF lists the servers allowed to send mail for the domain. Errors make receivers ignore it (permerror) and permissive endings authorise anyone. Spoofed messages using the domain are easier to deliver, and legitimate mail may fail DMARC alignment.

Recommended actions:

- Merge all SPF policies into a single TXT record starting with v=spf1.
- End the record with "-all" (or "~all" while validating senders); never use "+all".
- Pair SPF with DKIM and an enforced DMARC policy.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208>
- <https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/bod-18-01-enhance-email-and-web-security>
- <https://www.m3aawg.org/sites/default/files/m3aawg_parked_domains_bp-2015-12.pdf>

### DNS-005 — DNSSEC not enabled

| Field                      | Value |
| -------------------------- | ----- |
| Version                    | 1     |
| Category                   | `dns` |
| Default severity           | low   |
| Default confidence         | high  |
| Observation kinds required | `dns` |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns` |

**Evidence required.** Successful DS lookup for the apex (the DNSKEY lookup, when successful, distinguishes "unsigned" from "signed but no DS at the parent").

**Detection.** The parent zone publishes no DS record for the apex, so DNS answers cannot be validated.

**Resolution.** A DS record for the apex is published.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Enable DNSSEC for example.com_

DNSSEC signs DNS data so resolvers can detect spoofed or tampered answers. Without DNSSEC, users of validating resolvers get no protection against cache poisoning or on-path DNS tampering for this domain.

Recommended actions:

- Enable DNSSEC signing at the DNS provider (most managed providers support automatic signing and key rollover).
- Publish the provided DS record at the registrar.
- Verify the chain of trust and monitor for signature expiry.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4033>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9364>
- <https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/dnssec-what-is-it-why-important-2019-03-05-en>

### DNS-006 — No CAA record

| Field                      | Value         |
| -------------------------- | ------------- |
| Version                    | 1             |
| Category                   | `dns`         |
| Default severity           | informational |
| Default confidence         | high          |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`         |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`         |

**Evidence required.** Successful CAA lookup at the apex.

**Detection.** The apex publishes no CAA record, so any public CA may issue certificates for the domain.

**Resolution.** At least one CAA record is published at the apex.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Publish CAA records for example.com_

CAA records name the certificate authorities allowed to issue for the domain. Restricting issuance to the CAs you use reduces the chance of a mis-issued certificate for the domain.

Recommended actions:

- List the CAs currently issuing your certificates (check Certificate Transparency logs).
- Publish CAA records such as example.com. CAA 0 issue "<ca-domain>" for each, and 0 issuewild if wildcards are used.
- Optionally add an iodef contact to receive violation reports.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8659>
- <https://cabforum.org/working-groups/server/baseline-requirements/>

### DNS-007 — Monitoring-only DMARC policy

| Field                      | Value   |
| -------------------------- | ------- |
| Version                    | 1       |
| Category                   | `email` |
| Default severity           | low     |
| Default confidence         | high    |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`   |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`   |

**Evidence required.** Successful TXT lookup at _dmarc.<apex>.

**Detection.** Exactly one DMARC record is published and its policy is p=none (monitoring only). Missing, duplicate or invalid records are DNS-003.

**Resolution.** The DMARC policy is quarantine or reject (or the record is missing/invalid, which DNS-003 reports instead).

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Enforce the DMARC policy for example.com_

A p=none policy only monitors; it does not ask receivers to reject or quarantine spoofed mail. Phishing that impersonates the domain is still delivered while the policy stays at p=none.

Recommended actions:

- Review the aggregate (rua) reports and fix SPF/DKIM alignment for every legitimate sender.
- Move to p=quarantine (optionally with pct= for a staged rollout), then to p=reject.
- Set sp= for subdomains that do not send mail.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7489>
- <https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/bod-18-01-enhance-email-and-web-security>
- <https://www.m3aawg.org/sites/default/files/m3aawg_parked_domains_bp-2015-12.pdf>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7505>

### DNS-008 — Subdomain takeover risk confirmed by provider response

| Field                      | Value |
| -------------------------- | ----- |
| Version                    | 1     |
| Category                   | `dns` |
| Default severity           | high  |
| Default confidence         | high  |
| Observation kinds required | `dns` |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns` |

**Evidence required.** Successful CNAME lookup for the hostname. DNS evidence: successful A and AAAA lookups (the resolver follows the chain; the worker records the chain end as canonicalName, also for NXDOMAIN). HTTP evidence: an http_availability response for the hostname carrying evidence.takeoverSignature (matched by the worker on the body it already reads; no extra request). Fingerprints: packages/rules/src/takeover-fingerprints.ts, curated from can-i-take-over-xyz (Vulnerable / Edge case entries only).

**Detection.** Either (a) the CNAME chain leaves the monitored domain for a provider whose fingerprint says a dangling NXDOMAIN name can be re-registered by anyone (Azure, Elastic Beanstalk), neither A nor AAAA returns an address, and the answer was NXDOMAIN — confidence medium; or (b) the HTTP response for the hostname matches that same provider's "unclaimed resource" signature while the CNAME chain points at the provider — confidence high (medium when the provider is used without a CNAME, e.g. GitHub Pages apex A records). Severity is always high. Nothing is claimed or registered. DNS-002 (the weaker, unconfirmed signal) is still reported independently. Note: the scope validator refuses web checks for CNAME chains that leave the domain, so path (b) with a CNAME only applies if that policy changes; today the HTTP path applies to hosts without a CNAME.

**Resolution.** A complete successful DNS check (CNAME plus A/AAAA) no longer shows the NXDOMAIN evidence and, where the provider is only confirmable over HTTP (or the host has no CNAME), a successful HTTP response for the host in the same job shows no signature. Failed or incomplete checks never resolve.

**Sample advisory** (for `shop.example.com`): _Remove or re-claim the dangling record for shop.example.com_

shop.example.com points at Microsoft Azure where the referenced resource appears to be unclaimed. This is the classic precondition for a subdomain takeover. Whoever claims the resource can serve arbitrary content (phishing, malware) under your hostname, read cookies scoped to the parent domain, and obtain trusted certificates for it.

Recommended actions:

- Treat this as urgent: confirm with the owner whether the service is still in use.
- If it is not, delete the DNS record for shop.example.com now (and any records that point at it).
- If it is, re-create or re-claim the resource on Microsoft Azure under your organisation's account immediately, and use the provider's domain verification feature where available.
- Check whether the hostname already serves unexpected content; if so, handle it as a security incident.
- Add DNS cleanup to the decommissioning checklist for cloud and SaaS resources.

References:

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/subdomain-takeover>
- <https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/02-Configuration_and_Deployment_Management_Testing/10-Test_for_Subdomain_Takeover>
- <https://github.com/EdOverflow/can-i-take-over-xyz>

### EMAIL-001 — No MTA-STS policy for a mail domain

| Field                      | Value   |
| -------------------------- | ------- |
| Version                    | 1       |
| Category                   | `email` |
| Default severity           | low     |
| Default confidence         | high    |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`   |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`   |

**Evidence required.** Successful apex MX lookup listing a real exchanger and a successful TXT lookup at _mta-sts.<apex> (NXDOMAIN/NODATA count as "no record"). Only the DNS record is checked; the HTTPS policy file is never fetched.

**Detection.** The domain receives mail (MX present, not a null MX) but no TXT record at _mta-sts.<apex> begins with v=STSv1. Malformed or duplicate records are EMAIL-002.

**Resolution.** A v=STSv1 record is published at _mta-sts.<apex>, or the apex MX lookup shows the domain no longer receives mail.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Publish an MTA-STS policy for example.com_

MTA-STS lets a receiving domain require authenticated TLS for inbound SMTP, so senders refuse to deliver over downgraded or spoofed connections. Inbound mail can be read or redirected by an attacker able to tamper with the network path or DNS responses seen by sending servers.

Recommended actions:

- Host the policy at https://mta-sts.example.com/.well-known/mta-sts.txt listing your MX hosts, starting with "mode: testing".
- Publish TXT "v=STSv1; id=<version>" at _mta-sts.example.com (change id whenever the policy changes).
- Publish a TLS-RPT record to receive failure reports, then move the policy to "mode: enforce".
- Make sure every MX host presents a valid certificate for its name.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8460>
- <https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/email-security-and-anti-spoofing>

### EMAIL-002 — MTA-STS record malformed

| Field                      | Value   |
| -------------------------- | ------- |
| Version                    | 1       |
| Category                   | `email` |
| Default severity           | low     |
| Default confidence         | high    |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`   |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`   |

**Evidence required.** Successful apex MX lookup listing a real exchanger and a successful TXT lookup at _mta-sts.<apex>.

**Detection.** More than one TXT record at _mta-sts.<apex> begins with v=STSv1, or the single record has no valid id= (1–32 letters or digits). Senders then treat the domain as having no MTA-STS policy (RFC 8461 §3.1).

**Resolution.** Exactly one well-formed v=STSv1 record (or none — EMAIL-001 then applies), or the domain no longer receives mail.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Fix the MTA-STS record for example.com_

The MTA-STS DNS record must be a single TXT record "v=STSv1; id=<1–32 alphanumerics>". Until it is valid, senders apply no MTA-STS protection to inbound mail.

Recommended actions:

- Keep exactly one TXT record at _mta-sts.example.com starting with "v=STSv1;".
- Give it an id= of 1–32 letters or digits, e.g. a date stamp such as 20261029T0000; change it whenever the policy file changes.
- Verify the policy file at https://mta-sts.example.com/.well-known/mta-sts.txt is reachable over HTTPS.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461>

### EMAIL-003 — No TLS reporting (TLS-RPT) for a mail domain

| Field                      | Value         |
| -------------------------- | ------------- |
| Version                    | 1             |
| Category                   | `email`       |
| Default severity           | informational |
| Default confidence         | high          |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`         |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`         |

**Evidence required.** Successful apex MX lookup listing a real exchanger and a successful TXT lookup at _smtp._tls.<apex>.

**Detection.** The domain receives mail but has no usable TLS-RPT record: none beginning with v=TLSRPTv1, more than one, or a record without a valid rua= (mailto: or https: URIs).

**Resolution.** Exactly one v=TLSRPTv1 record with a valid rua= is published, or the domain no longer receives mail.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Publish a TLS-RPT record for example.com_

TLS-RPT gives the domain daily reports of TLS failures seen by sending mail servers. Without reports, MTA-STS/DANE misconfigurations and TLS downgrade attempts go unnoticed.

Recommended actions:

- Publish one TXT record at _smtp._tls.example.com: "v=TLSRPTv1; rua=mailto:<reporting address>".
- Route the reports to a mailbox or a reporting service that someone reviews.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8460>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461>

### EMAIL-004 — No DKIM key found at common selectors

| Field                      | Value         |
| -------------------------- | ------------- |
| Version                    | 1             |
| Category                   | `email`       |
| Default severity           | informational |
| Default confidence         | low           |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`         |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`         |

**Evidence required.** Successful apex MX lookup listing a real exchanger, and successful TXT lookups for every DKIM selector the worker queried (<selector>._domainkey.<apex>, a fixed list of common selectors; CNAME-delegated selectors are followed by the resolver). Any failed selector lookup skips the rule.

**Detection.** The domain has MX records but none of the queried common selectors publishes a DKIM key (a TXT record with a non-empty p=). DKIM selectors cannot be enumerated through DNS, so a domain using a custom or dated selector (e.g. Mimecast) is reported here although it signs mail: confidence is low.

**Resolution.** A DKIM key is found at one of the queried selectors, or the domain no longer receives mail.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Confirm DKIM signing for example.com_

DKIM signs outgoing mail so receivers can verify it was sent by an authorised system and not altered. Unsigned mail is more likely to be rejected or filtered, and DMARC cannot pass for forwarded mail.

Recommended actions:

- Ask the mail administrator which DKIM selectors are in use; if one exists, no action is needed (accept the finding).
- Otherwise enable DKIM signing in each sending service (mail platform, marketing and ticketing tools) and publish the provided keys.
- Use RSA keys of at least 2048 bits (or Ed25519 alongside RSA).

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6376>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8301>
- <https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/email-security-and-anti-spoofing>

### EMAIL-005 — Weak or revoked DKIM key

| Field                      | Value   |
| -------------------------- | ------- |
| Version                    | 1       |
| Category                   | `email` |
| Default severity           | medium  |
| Default confidence         | high    |
| Observation kinds required | `dns`   |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `dns`   |

**Evidence required.** Successful TXT lookup at <selector>._domainkey.<apex> for one of the common selectors the worker queries.

**Detection.** A published DKIM RSA key has a modulus shorter than 1024 bits (medium: such keys can be factored and RFC 8301 forbids verifying them), or the key record has an empty p= (informational: the key was revoked; harmless, reported as clean-up). One finding per selector.

**Resolution.** The selector publishes an RSA key of at least 1024 bits or a non-RSA key, or no longer publishes a key record.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Replace the weak DKIM key for example.com_

DKIM RSA keys shorter than 1024 bits are considered breakable and are not accepted by modern receivers. A factored key lets anyone sign mail that passes DKIM for the domain; meanwhile legitimate mail signed with it fails DKIM.

Recommended actions:

- Generate a new 2048-bit RSA key pair in the sending service, publish it under a new selector, and switch signing to it.
- Then revoke the old key by publishing an empty p= at s1._domainkey.example.com, and later remove the record.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6376>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8301>

### EXP-001 — Newly exposed TCP port

| Field                      | Value       |
| -------------------------- | ----------- |
| Version                    | 1           |
| Category                   | `exposure`  |
| Default severity           | low         |
| Default confidence         | high        |
| Observation kinds required | `port`      |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `tcp_ports` |

**Evidence required.** Successful `port` observations of the current job, and successful `port` observations of the same address from an earlier successful job (`previous`) as the baseline.

**Detection.** A port is open now on an address that has a baseline (a successful earlier port observation of that address), and the same address+port was absent, closed or filtered in the baseline. The first scan of an address establishes the baseline and raises nothing. Low; informational when the port is also an administrative service (EXP-002 carries the severity).

**Resolution.** A successful observation shows the address+port closed or filtered. While the port stays open the finding stays active (it records the change until reviewed). A user with `findings:triage` can also resolve it manually after review.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Confirm the newly exposed port is intended_

sample/tcp became reachable from the internet since the previous scan. Unplanned exposure is a common way services end up reachable without the hardening, patching or monitoring expected of internet-facing systems.

Recommended actions:

- Identify the owner of the service and confirm the exposure is intentional (change ticket, deployment).
- If unintended, close it at the host firewall or cloud security group and re-scan.
- If intended, make sure it is patched, authenticated and monitored, then acknowledge the finding.

References:

- <https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/cis-controls-list>
- <https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Attack_Surface_Analysis_Cheat_Sheet.html>
- <https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-41/rev-1/final>

### EXP-002 — Public administrative service violating the exposure policy

| Field                      | Value       |
| -------------------------- | ----------- |
| Version                    | 1           |
| Category                   | `exposure`  |
| Default severity           | high        |
| Default confidence         | medium      |
| Observation kinds required | `port`      |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `tcp_ports` |

**Evidence required.** Successful `port` observations (state) and, when the profile runs `service_identification`, the Nmap service/product in evidence.

**Detection.** An open port matches an entry of the exposure policy (`administrativeServices`: port → service, severity). Severity is the policy entry's severity. Confidence high when Nmap's probe identified the matching service, medium when only the port number matches. Accepted exceptions are handled as accepted risk on the finding.

**Resolution.** A successful observation shows the address+port closed or filtered.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Remove public access to administrative service_

administrative service on sample is reachable from the internet, contrary to the exposure policy. Internet-reachable administrative and data services are routinely targeted by automated password guessing and exploitation of known vulnerabilities; exposure of data stores can lead to data loss if authentication is weak or missing.

Recommended actions:

- Restrict the port at the firewall or cloud security group to known management networks, or close it.
- Put administrative access behind a VPN, bastion host or identity-aware proxy instead of exposing it directly.
- If the exposure is required, enforce strong authentication, keep the software patched, monitor access logs, and record an accepted-risk decision with a review date.

References:

- <https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/cis-controls-list>
- <https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-41/rev-1/final>
- <https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog>
- <https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/applications/>

### HTTP-001 — Website served without HTTPS

| Field                      | Value                               |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Version                    | 1                                   |
| Category                   | `http`                              |
| Default severity           | medium                              |
| Default confidence         | high                                |
| Observation kinds required | —                                   |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `http_availability`, `http_headers` |

**Evidence required.** For the hostname: the `https://<host>/` observation and, when HTTPS gave no response, the `http://<host>/` observation of the same job. A response is a status code on a `success` or `partial` observation (a refused redirect does not undo the response that carried it). Declares no required kinds because the triggering evidence is a failed HTTPS attempt.

**Detection.** `https://<host>/` reached an address but got no HTTP response (error/timeout, no status code) while `http://<host>/` returned an HTTP status (including a redirect to another domain). If neither answered, there is no finding (not a web host).

**Resolution.** `https://<host>/` returned an HTTP status in the current job.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Serve the site over HTTPS_

example.com answers over plain HTTP but HTTPS does not respond. Traffic, cookies and form data travel unencrypted and can be read or modified on the network; browsers label the site "Not secure".

Recommended actions:

- Enable HTTPS (port 443) with a publicly trusted certificate (e.g. via ACME) on the server, load balancer or CDN.
- Then redirect all plain-HTTP requests to HTTPS with a 301 and enable HSTS.
- If the hostname only forwards to another domain, terminate HTTPS for it too (or remove it if unused), so the redirect itself is protected.

References:

- <https://infosec.mozilla.org/guidelines/web_security>
- <https://wiki.mozilla.org/Security/Server_Side_TLS>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797>

### HTTP-002 — HTTP does not redirect to HTTPS

| Field                      | Value                               |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Version                    | 1                                   |
| Category                   | `http`                              |
| Default severity           | low                                 |
| Default confidence         | high                                |
| Observation kinds required | —                                   |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `http_availability`, `http_headers` |

**Evidence required.** `http://<host>/` observation whose first hop returned a status (evidence.hops[0].status). The worker only requests plain HTTP when HTTPS gave no response, so this rule is evaluated only for such hosts.

**Detection.** The first plain-HTTP response is 2xx (content served over HTTP), or the in-domain redirect chain ends in a 2xx response on an http:// URL. A redirect to https://, or to another domain (refused as redirect_out_of_scope — the hostname forwards elsewhere), is not flagged.

**Resolution.** The first plain-HTTP response is a redirect (3xx) or a non-2xx status, or the chain ends on HTTPS.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Redirect plain HTTP to HTTPS_

example.com serves content over plain HTTP. Users reaching the site by typing the name or via old links use an unencrypted connection that can be read or modified.

Recommended actions:

- Make sure HTTPS is available first (see HTTP-001 if reported).
- Answer every plain-HTTP request with a 301 redirect to the same path on https://.
- Enable HSTS once HTTPS works everywhere so browsers skip plain HTTP entirely.

References:

- <https://infosec.mozilla.org/guidelines/web_security>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797>
- <https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Strict_Transport_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html>

### HTTP-003 — HSTS not enabled

| Field                      | Value                               |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Version                    | 1                                   |
| Category                   | `http`                              |
| Default severity           | low                                 |
| Default confidence         | high                                |
| Observation kinds required | `http`                              |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `http_availability`, `http_headers` |

**Evidence required.** A `success` `https://<host>/` observation whose final response is HTTPS, with hstsEnabled (Strict-Transport-Security with max-age > 0 on the final response).

**Detection.** The final HTTPS response has no valid Strict-Transport-Security header (hstsEnabled = false). Hosts without HTTPS are covered by HTTP-001 instead. The header is read from the final response of the in-domain redirect chain.

**Resolution.** A successful HTTPS observation shows hstsEnabled = true.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Enable HTTP Strict Transport Security_

example.com does not send a valid Strict-Transport-Security header. Visitors can be downgraded to plain HTTP on hostile networks (SSL stripping) before the redirect to HTTPS happens.

Recommended actions:

- Send `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` on all HTTPS responses (start with a short max-age, then increase).
- Only add includeSubDomains once every subdomain serves HTTPS; consider HSTS preload afterwards.
- Keep the redirect from HTTP to HTTPS in place.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797>
- <https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Strict_Transport_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html>
- <https://infosec.mozilla.org/guidelines/web_security>
- <https://hstspreload.org/>

### HTTP-004 — Recommended security headers missing

| Field                      | Value          |
| -------------------------- | -------------- |
| Version                    | 1              |
| Category                   | `http`         |
| Default severity           | informational  |
| Default confidence         | high           |
| Observation kinds required | `http`         |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `http_headers` |

**Evidence required.** A `success` http observation with final status 200 and evidence.securityHeaders (captured only when the profile runs `http_headers`). HTTPS observations are preferred over plain HTTP.

**Detection.** Any of Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options (or CSP frame-ancestors) or Referrer-Policy is missing on the final 200 response. One finding per hostname listing the missing headers. Low when framing protection is missing (neither X-Frame-Options nor frame-ancestors), otherwise informational.

**Resolution.** A qualifying observation shows all four headers present.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Add recommended HTTP security headers_

example.com is missing recommended security headers. Missing headers remove browser-side protections that limit the impact of cross-site scripting, clickjacking and information leakage through referrers.

Recommended actions:

- Set the headers at the web server, application or CDN so every HTML response carries them.

References:

- <https://owasp.org/www-project-secure-headers/>
- <https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html>
- <https://infosec.mozilla.org/guidelines/web_security>

### HTTP-005 — Software version disclosed in HTTP headers

| Field                      | Value          |
| -------------------------- | -------------- |
| Version                    | 1              |
| Category                   | `http`         |
| Default severity           | informational  |
| Default confidence         | high           |
| Observation kinds required | `http`         |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `http_headers` |

**Evidence required.** An http observation with a response and evidence.server / evidence.xPoweredBy captured (profile runs `http_headers`). Raised from `success` or `partial` (the header came from a real response); resolved only from `success`.

**Detection.** The Server or X-Powered-By header contains a dotted version number (e.g. `Apache/2.4.41`, `PHP/8.1.2`). Informational: this is disclosure, not a confirmed vulnerability.

**Resolution.** A successful observation shows neither header carries a version number.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Stop advertising software versions_

example.com reveals software versions in its HTTP headers. Version strings make it cheaper to find known vulnerabilities for the exact software in use. Disclosure alone is not a vulnerability; patching matters more than hiding.

Recommended actions:

- Confirm the disclosed software is on a supported, patched version.
- Suppress version details (e.g. nginx `server_tokens off`, Apache `ServerTokens Prod` / `ServerSignature Off`, PHP `expose_php = Off`).
- Remove X-Powered-By at the application or reverse proxy.

References:

- <https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Information_Gathering/02-Fingerprint_Web_Server>
- <https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html>

### LOOK-001 — Lookalike domain registered

| Field                      | Value       |
| -------------------------- | ----------- |
| Version                    | 1           |
| Category                   | `asset`     |
| Default severity           | medium      |
| Default confidence         | medium      |
| Observation kinds required | —           |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `lookalike` |

**Evidence required.** Lookalike observations of a brand-monitoring job (public-resolver NS/SOA, A, AAAA and MX lookups of server-generated candidates) and the job's candidate list with its completeness.

**Detection.** A lookalike candidate of the domain exists in DNS (NS or SOA at the candidate; A/AAAA/MX for subdomain-split candidates). One finding per candidate (component = the candidate). Severity: medium with mail exchangers (MX, not a null MX), low with only web addresses (A/AAAA), informational when only delegated (NS/SOA).

**Resolution.** A complete brand run (every candidate checked; the time budget was not exhausted) no longer finds the candidate registered. Candidates that failed to resolve in that run (SERVFAIL, timeout) and incomplete runs never resolve.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Review the lookalike domain sample_

sample resembles example.com and is registered. Lookalike domains are used for phishing, invoice fraud and brand impersonation, but many are parked or harmless. Customers, suppliers and staff can mistake a lookalike for the real domain: e-mail from it can request payments or credentials, and a website on it can imitate yours. Mail-capable lookalikes are the most common setup for business e-mail compromise.

Recommended actions:

- Check who holds it: look up the registrar and registrant in RDAP/WHOIS and confirm it is not a registration made by your own organisation or a partner.
- If it is yours, record it as a defensive registration (accept the risk, or add it to the domain inventory) so it is not reported again as a threat.
- If it is unknown, watch it: changes to its MX or web records are worth an alert to your mail-security and SOC teams; consider blocking it on your mail gateway and web proxy.
- If it is used for phishing or impersonation, report it to the registrar abuse contact (from RDAP) and the hosting provider, and consider a UDRP complaint for trademark abuse.
- Consider registering the most convincing variants of your main domains defensively.

References:

- <https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1583/001/>
- <https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/abuse-2014-01-29-en>
- <https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/avoiding-social-engineering-and-phishing-attacks>

### REG-001 — Domain registration expiry within 30 days

| Field                      | Value          |
| -------------------------- | -------------- |
| Version                    | 1              |
| Category                   | `registration` |
| Default severity           | high           |
| Default confidence         | high           |
| Observation kinds required | `registration` |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `rdap`         |

**Evidence required.** Successful RDAP registration observation with dataStatus available or redacted and an expiry date.

**Detection.** The registry expiry date is within 60 days of the evaluation time: passed → critical (expired, possibly in a grace period), ≤ 30 days → high, ≤ 60 days → medium.

**Resolution.** The registry expiry date is more than 60 days away (the registration was renewed).

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Renew the registration of example.com_

The domain registration is close to, or past, its registry expiry date. An expired domain stops resolving, interrupting web and e-mail, and a dropped domain can be re-registered by a third party who would then receive its traffic and mail.

Recommended actions:

- Renew the domain with the registrar now, for several years if possible.
- Enable auto-renew and keep the payment method and registrar contact addresses current.
- Confirm the new expiry date is visible in RDAP after renewal (the finding resolves on the next scan).
- Track registrar ownership and renewal responsibility in the asset inventory.

References:

- <https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/errp-2013-02-28-en>
- <https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/epp-status-codes-2014-06-16-en>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9083>

### REG-002 — Unexpected registrar or nameserver change

| Field                      | Value          |
| -------------------------- | -------------- |
| Version                    | 1              |
| Category                   | `registration` |
| Default severity           | medium         |
| Default confidence         | medium         |
| Observation kinds required | `registration` |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `rdap`         |

**Evidence required.** Successful RDAP registration observations (dataStatus available or redacted) in the current job and the previous successful job, with the compared field present in both.

**Detection.** The registrar name (compared case- and whitespace-insensitively) or the registration nameserver set differs from the previous observation. Components: registrar, nameservers. There is no change-approval workflow yet, so every change is reported for review.

**Resolution.** Not auto-resolved: a change is an event that needs review, so the finding stays open until an analyst resolves or accepts it. A user with `findings:triage` can also resolve it manually after review.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Review the registrar change for example.com_

The sponsoring registrar of the domain changed since the previous scan. Control of the registration or delegation means control of the domain: its web traffic, e-mail and the ability to obtain certificates for it.

Recommended actions:

- Confirm with the domain owner that the change was planned (transfer or DNS migration ticket).
- If unplanned: contact the registrar immediately, secure the registrar account (credentials, MFA, contact e-mail) and request the change be reversed.
- Enable clientTransferProhibited / registrar lock and, for critical domains, registry lock.
- Once reviewed, resolve the finding (or accept it) in ExDomainVault.

References:

- <https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/transfer-policy-2016-06-01-en>
- <https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-19-01-mitigate-dns-infrastructure-tampering>
- <https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/epp-status-codes-2014-06-16-en>
- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9083>

### SOFT-001 — End-of-life software exposed

| Field                      | Value                                                         |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Version                    | 1                                                             |
| Category                   | `software`                                                    |
| Default severity           | medium                                                        |
| Default confidence         | medium                                                        |
| Observation kinds required | —                                                             |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `http_headers`, `http_availability`, `service_identification` |

**Evidence required.** A successful http observation with evidence.server / evidence.xPoweredBy (profile runs `http_headers`) or a successful open port observation with evidence.product / evidence.version (`service_identification`), plus end-of-life cycles from endoflife.date in `context.softwareIntel`. Without feed data the rule produces nothing.

**Detection.** A catalogue product reports a version whose release cycle (the longest numeric cycle that is a dotted prefix of the version) is end of life upstream: the feed says `eol: true` or the EOL date is on or before the evaluation time. Severity medium; high when the cycle has been end of life for more than 365 days AND (the evidence is service identification OR the product is PHP, Apache HTTP Server, nginx, OpenSSL or IIS). Confidence medium; low when the banner names a distribution (fixes may be backported).

**Resolution.** A successful observation of the same source and location reports the product with a version whose cycle is not end of life. A hidden version, a missing product, a cycle the feed does not know, or failed/partial evidence is unknown and does not resolve. A user with `findings:triage` can also resolve it manually after review.

**Sample advisory** (for `www.example.com`): _Upgrade PHP to a supported release_

www.example.com reports PHP 7.4.3-4ubuntu2.19 (release cycle 7.4), which is end of life upstream. Because the banner names Ubuntu, the distribution may still ship security fixes for it. End-of-life software stops receiving upstream security fixes, so newly found vulnerabilities stay open. The finding is based on the version the server reports; it does not confirm a vulnerability or an attack.

Recommended actions:

- Confirm which PHP version actually runs on this host.
- The banner names Ubuntu. Check the Ubuntu security tracker / support status for this package: a supported distribution release may carry the fixes despite the old upstream version. If it does, record that and resolve the finding manually.
- Plan an upgrade to a supported PHP release cycle and track it to completion.
- Hide version details in banners once patched (this reduces disclosure, not risk).

References:

- <https://endoflife.date/php>
- <https://www.php.net/supported-versions.php>
- <https://ubuntu.com/about/release-cycle>
- <https://owasp.org/Top10/A06_2021-Vulnerable_and_Outdated_Components/>

### SOFT-002 — Version possibly affected by a known-exploited vulnerability

| Field                      | Value                                                         |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Version                    | 1                                                             |
| Category                   | `software`                                                    |
| Default severity           | high                                                          |
| Default confidence         | medium                                                        |
| Observation kinds required | —                                                             |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `http_headers`, `http_availability`, `service_identification` |

**Evidence required.** A successful http observation with evidence.server / evidence.xPoweredBy (`http_headers`) or a successful open port observation with evidence.product / evidence.version (`service_identification`), plus CISA KEV advisories with NVD affected version ranges in `context.softwareIntel`. Advisories without ranges are ignored. Without feed data the rule produces nothing.

**Detection.** A catalogue product reports a version (at least two numeric segments, e.g. not `Apache/2`) inside ANY affected range of a CISA KEV CVE for that product. One finding per location, product and CVE. Severity high; critical when the CVSS base score is 9.0 or more or KEV marks the CVE as used in ransomware campaigns. Confidence medium; low when the banner names a distribution (fixes may be backported). Wording: possibly affected — verify; never a claim of compromise.

**Resolution.** A successful observation of the same source and location reports the product with a version outside every affected range of that CVE. A hidden or too-coarse version, a missing product, failed/partial evidence, or a CVE no longer in the feed does not resolve. A user with `findings:triage` can also resolve it manually after review.

**Sample advisory** (for `www.example.com`): _Verify and patch PHP for CVE-2024-4577_

www.example.com reports PHP 8.1.2, which falls in the affected range of CVE-2024-4577, a vulnerability CISA lists as exploited in the wild. This is possibly affected, not confirmed. Vulnerabilities in the KEV catalogue are actively used by attackers, so an affected internet-facing service is a priority to verify. The match is based on the version the server reports; backported fixes or configuration may mean the host is not affected, and nothing here indicates that the host was attacked.

Recommended actions:

- Confirm the exact PHP version and build installed on this host.
- If affected, apply the vendor fix or mitigation for CVE-2024-4577 without delay (see the KEV entry for required actions).
- If the host is not affected (backport, feature not in use), record the evidence and resolve the finding manually.

References:

- <https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog>
- <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-4577>
- <https://www.php.net/supported-versions.php>

### TLS-001 — Expired or not-yet-valid TLS certificate

| Field                      | Value                                  |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Version                    | 1                                      |
| Category                   | `tls`                                  |
| Default severity           | high                                   |
| Default confidence         | high                                   |
| Observation kinds required | `tls`                                  |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `tls_certificate`, `tls_configuration` |

**Evidence required.** Successful `tls` observations (certificate read and parsed) for the hostname and port, with notBefore/notAfter.

**Detection.** Any address serving the hostname presents a certificate whose notAfter is before the evaluation time (expired) or whose notBefore is after it (not yet valid). One finding per hostname and port; evidence lists the affected addresses.

**Resolution.** Every current observation for the hostname and port succeeded and every certificate is inside its validity period.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Renew the expired certificate_

example.com:sample presents an expired certificate. Visitors receive browser security warnings or cannot connect; automated clients fail. Users trained to click through warnings become easier to deceive.

Recommended actions:

- Issue and install a renewed certificate on every listed address (and any load balancer or CDN edge).
- Automate renewal (e.g. ACME) and alert at least 30 days before expiry.
- Reload or restart the TLS terminator so it serves the new certificate, then re-scan.

References:

- <https://wiki.mozilla.org/Security/Server_Side_TLS>
- <https://cabforum.org/working-groups/server/baseline-requirements/documents/>

### TLS-002 — Certificate hostname mismatch

| Field                      | Value                                  |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Version                    | 1                                      |
| Category                   | `tls`                                  |
| Default severity           | medium                                 |
| Default confidence         | high                                   |
| Observation kinds required | `tls`                                  |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `tls_certificate`, `tls_configuration` |

**Evidence required.** Successful `tls` observations with `hostnameMatches` (RFC 6125 matching against dNSName SANs, computed by the worker).

**Detection.** Any address serving the hostname presents a certificate whose subjectAltNames do not cover the hostname (hostnameMatches = false). Medium; high when the chain is also untrusted for another reason (self-signed, unknown CA).

**Resolution.** Every current observation for the hostname and port succeeded and every certificate matches the hostname.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Serve a certificate that covers the hostname_

example.com:sample presents a certificate that does not include the hostname. Visitors see certificate warnings or cannot connect; users who learn to ignore warnings are easier to target with real interception attempts.

Recommended actions:

- Issue a certificate whose subjectAltName includes example.com (wildcards cover exactly one label).
- Check SNI and virtual host configuration on every listed address so the right certificate is selected.
- If the hostname is no longer used, remove its DNS records instead of leaving it pointed at a shared server.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6125>
- <https://cabforum.org/working-groups/server/baseline-requirements/documents/>
- <https://wiki.mozilla.org/Security/Server_Side_TLS>

### TLS-003 — Certificate expiry within 14 days

| Field                      | Value                                  |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Version                    | 1                                      |
| Category                   | `tls`                                  |
| Default severity           | medium                                 |
| Default confidence         | high                                   |
| Observation kinds required | `tls`                                  |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `tls_certificate`, `tls_configuration` |

**Evidence required.** Successful `tls` observations with notAfter.

**Detection.** A currently valid certificate (notAfter not before the evaluation time) expires within 14 days (0 ≤ remaining ≤ 14 days, inclusive). Medium; high when 3 days or fewer remain. Already-expired certificates are TLS-001.

**Resolution.** Every current observation for the hostname and port succeeded and every currently valid certificate has more than 14 days remaining (an expired one moves to TLS-001).

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Renew the certificate before it expires_

example.com:sample presents a certificate that expires soon. An expired certificate causes browser warnings and failed API connections, interrupting the service.

Recommended actions:

- Renew and deploy the certificate on every listed address now.
- If renewal is automated (ACME), check why it has not run: failed challenges, rate limits or a stopped renewal job.
- Alert on certificates with fewer than 30 days remaining.

References:

- <https://wiki.mozilla.org/Security/Server_Side_TLS>
- <https://cabforum.org/working-groups/server/baseline-requirements/documents/>

### TLS-004 — Weak or unsupported TLS configuration

| Field                      | Value                                  |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Version                    | 1                                      |
| Category                   | `tls`                                  |
| Default severity           | medium                                 |
| Default confidence         | medium                                 |
| Observation kinds required | `tls`                                  |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `tls_certificate`, `tls_configuration` |

**Evidence required.** Successful `tls` observations with protocolVersion (the version negotiated by the worker). Per-version enumeration (`tls_configuration`) is not implemented by the worker yet.

**Detection.** The negotiated protocol is SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 (deprecated by RFC 8996). Only the negotiated version is known, so a server that also accepts old versions but prefers TLS 1.2+ is not detected (confidence medium). The worker requires TLS 1.2+ for its handshake, so a server offering only old versions currently fails the handshake (error observation) instead of producing evidence here.

**Resolution.** Every current observation for the hostname and port succeeded and negotiated TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Disable deprecated TLS protocol versions_

example.com:sample negotiates a deprecated TLS protocol version. Old protocol versions have known cryptographic weaknesses and fail compliance requirements (e.g. PCI DSS); modern clients increasingly refuse them.

Recommended actions:

- Allow only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 on the server, load balancer and CDN.
- Apply the Mozilla 'intermediate' configuration for your server software.
- Re-scan to confirm TLS 1.2+ is negotiated on every address.

References:

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996>
- <https://wiki.mozilla.org/Security/Server_Side_TLS>
- <https://ssl-config.mozilla.org/>
- <https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Transport_Layer_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html>

### TLS-005 — Untrusted certificate chain

| Field                      | Value                                  |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Version                    | 1                                      |
| Category                   | `tls`                                  |
| Default severity           | medium                                 |
| Default confidence         | high                                   |
| Observation kinds required | `tls`                                  |
| Profile checks (any of)    | `tls_certificate`, `tls_configuration` |

**Evidence required.** Successful `tls` observations with evidence.trusted and, when untrusted, evidence.verifyError (OpenSSL verification message).

**Detection.** evidence.trusted = false with a verifyError that is not only a hostname mismatch, expiry or not-yet-valid (those are TLS-002/TLS-001): self-signed certificate, unknown CA or incomplete chain. Confidence high for recognised chain errors, medium for other messages.

**Resolution.** Every current observation for the hostname and port succeeded, and each is trusted or fails only for a reason covered by TLS-001/TLS-002.

**Sample advisory** (for `example.com`): _Serve a publicly trusted, complete certificate chain_

example.com:sample presents a certificate chain that public clients do not trust. Visitors see certificate warnings or cannot connect; API clients fail. Users trained to accept warnings are easier to deceive.

Recommended actions:

- Replace self-signed or private-CA certificates on public endpoints with certificates from a publicly trusted CA.
- Configure the server to send the full intermediate chain (leaf first, then intermediates; no root needed).
- Verify the result with an external TLS checker, then re-scan.

References:

- <https://cabforum.org/working-groups/server/baseline-requirements/documents/>
- <https://wiki.mozilla.org/Security/Server_Side_TLS>
- <https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Transport_Layer_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html>
